answer: From a skiff the surveyors sound the eelgrass meadows and count the shoots in every square they sample, entering the count in the mapping book. A willow meadow copied from another bay fails the book: at the prism of the shoot the grass must match the meadow's own bed, and a copied meadow belongs to another shore. Buying a false map means bribing a surveyor, faking a summer of soundings and paying 21,200, and the reef entry in the mapping book is read at every dredging, so a meadow whose shoots were never counted is closed.
